html:
A strong earthquake that struck northern Syria around Aleppo on 11 October 1138, during the wars of the Crusades. It is often listed among the deadliest earthquakes in history.

The worst damage was in the towns and castles between Aleppo and the coast. The citadel of Aleppo and its walls were damaged. The crusader castle of Harim collapsed, and the Muslim fortress of Atharib was wrecked, killing its garrison. It was part of a run of shocks from 1137 to 1139 along the great fault that runs from the Red Sea to southern Turkey, the same zone that later produced the 2023 Turkey and Syria earthquakes.

A chronicler writing three centuries later put the death toll at 230,000. Modern scholars think he merged several earthquakes, including one at Ganja in the Caucasus, and the real number is unknown. The quake hit while Zengi, the Turkish ruler of Aleppo and Mosul, was building the Muslim power that his son and later Saladin would turn against the crusaders. Aleppo recovered and later thrived as an Ottoman trading hub.
